 AN CHÚIRT UACHTARACH 

 THE SUPREME COURT 

 [2026] IESC 1 

 Record No. 2025/48 

 Dunne J. 

 Woulfe J. 

 Hogan J. 

 Collins J. 

 Donnelly J. 

   

 BETWEEN/ 

 PROTECT EAST MEATH LIMITED 

 Applicant/Appellant 

 -and- 

   

 MEATH COUNTY COUNCIL 

 Respondent 

   

 

 

 

 JUDGMENT of Mr. Justice Woulfe delivered on the 22 nd day of January, 2026 

 Introduction 

 1.              The appellant appeals the decision of the High Court (Nolan J.) which dismissed its application for judicial review, seeking inter alia , an order of mandamus 
 in circumstances where it asserts that the respondent (the "Council") failed to commence the process of making a Local Area Plan ("LAP") for an area in County Meath known as Laytown-Bettystown-Mornington-Donacarney ("East Meath") pursuant to s. 19(1)(b) and (c) of the Planning and Development Act, 2000 ("the 2000 Act"). The appellant is a nonprofit organisation whose mission is to ensure that future development in East Meath has the strongest possible environmental protection.  

 2.              The previous East Meath LAP 2014 - 2020 was adopted in July 2014, and expired in October 2020.  Under s. 19(1)(c) of the 2000 Act a planning authority was required to send and publish a notice of a proposal to make or amend a LAP at least every six years after the making of the previous LAP.  The Council failed to commence the statutory process within the time stipulated. 

 3.              The appellant corresponded with the Council in August 2023, calling upon it to commence the process or proceedings would issue.  The Council responded in September 2023 and stated that it had an indicative forward planning programme.  It maintained that there were other strategy plans of greater planning priority which first needed to be addressed, and that it had limited resources.  As the Council would later observe in its statement of opposition to these proceedings, East Meath is, in fact, in ninth place in a settlement hierarchy identified in the current Meath County Development Plan ("CDP") 2021-2027, so that, for example, it ranks behind towns and areas such as South Drogheda Environs, Navan and Maynooth, which are respectively ranked first, second and third in the settlement hierarchy.  The Council has pointed to the fact that work is ongoing in relation to these other settlements, so that, for example, the joint Maynooth/Clane LAP is effective from the 1 st April, 2025.  In passing, however, it might be observed that this sequence of priorities - commendable and understandable as it may be in terms of the allocation of resources - is nonetheless an internal matter for the Council, and it has no statutory foundation.  

 4.              Returning now to the chronological narrative, in November, 2023 the appellant noted that there was no commitment by the Council to commence the process of making a new LAP, and stated that there was no provision within the 2000 Act which made the preparation of an LAP contingent upon the availability of resources.   

 5.              These judicial review proceedings were commenced in June, 2024, and in October, 2024 the Council indicated an intention to concede the proceedings to the extent that it would consent to a declaration that it was in breach of its statutory obligations, with the balance of the proceedings to be adjourned generally.  The appellant did not accept this proposal, and its claim for an order of mandamus proceeded to trial.    

 The High Court    

 6.              In his judgment delivered on the 14 th March, 2025, ( [2025] IEHC 149 ), Nolan J. highlighted that an order of mandamus is a discretionary remedy, and adopted some statements made by Keane J. in Brady v. Cavan County Council [1999] 4 IR 99 (" Brady ") to that effect.  He held that there may be exceptional circumstances which justify the Court in exercising its discretion and refusing mandamus .  One argument made by the Council was that certain sections of the Planning and Development Act, 2024 ("the 2024 Act") governing the adoption of LAPs would come into effect soon and, therefore, it would be something of a waste of time and money to prepare an LAP before that, given that the LAP would only be effective for a limited period of time.  That did not strike Nolan J. as a strong ground at all, and he agreed with the appellant that the Council must find the law as it is and not as it may be. 

 7.              Another issue relied on by the Council related to the loss of experienced staff and the failure of recruitment.  It seemed to Nolan J. that the Court should be very slow to intervene to direct the Council as to how to allocate its scarce resources, citing the decisions in Mulhaire v Cork County Council [2017] IEHC 288 (" Mulhaire "), Ward v Dublin South County Council [1996] 3 IR 195 (" Ward ") and McD v. Child and Family Agency [2024] IESC 6 (" McD "). 

 8.              One of the factors the trial judge took into consideration in the exercise of his discretion was the prejudice which might arise to the appellant. He concluded that in reality such prejudices which might arise to the appellant were somewhat theoretical.  When he balanced the potential prejudice on behalf of the appellant with the manifest and disruptive effect of the making of an order of mandamus against the Council, there was only one winner.    

 9.              Nolan J. did not accept the submission that the problems which the Council faced were not financial, nor was it special pleading.  He felt that if the qualified people were not available at the salary offered, then it was a question of lack of finance linked to a question of lack of expertise, making it very difficult for the Council to achieve what it was statutorily obliged to achieve.  Nor did he accept the submission that the Council had applied its resources to other non-statutory obligations at the expense of its statutory obligations.  As he had set out earlier, for the Court to involve itself in such matters would be to engage in micro-managing the work of the Council, or to put it another way, as Laffoy J. said in Ward , these were matters which fell outside the parameters of judicial review. 

 10.          Nolan J. concluded that it would be unjust for the Court to order, by way of mandamus , the preparation of an LAP for one specific part of County Meath, to the exclusion of the rest of the County, thereby dictating its own settlement hierarchy.  He accepted that the matters raised by the Council, when taken together, amounted to exceptional circumstances.  He therefore refused the application for mandamus .    

 Determination 

 11.          Following the High Court judgment, the appellant applied for leave to appeal to this Court and was granted leave by a determination dated the 23 rd May, 2025 ([2025] IESCDET 69). The Court was satisfied that a matter of general public importance did arise in relation to the Court's power to make an order of mandamus against a planning authority which has failed to comply with a mandatory obligation under the planning legislation, and as to the extent of the discretion to decline to do so. The Court felt that it might be that aspects of the reasoning in Brady might need to be re-assessed given the passage of time and developments in the case law, as suggested by Hogan J. in McD .  It was in the public interest that this Court should now consider whether any such re-assessment was in fact necessary.  The Court was further satisfied that the threshold of exceptional circumstances for the appellant to take a "leapfrog appeal" had been met in the circumstances of this case, where the outcome of the appeal might afford greater legal certainty in this area. 

 Submissions in this Appeal 

 Submissions of the Appellant 

 12.          The appellant firstly submits that notwithstanding the Council's concession of a declaration that it is in breach of its statutory obligations, it has said that it is not prepared to take any steps on foot of that declaration, and this is inappropriate and inherently contradictory. In the absence of implementation such a declaration is effectively meaningless and serves to compound the Council's default on its statutory duty.  Pointedly, the Council in conceding declaratory relief did not cite lack of resources as the basis for its concession, but cites this as an excuse for not acting on that declaration.  

 13.          The appellant outlines that the only issue is whether an order of mandamus is required to be made in circumstances where the Council has repeatedly refused to commence the preparation of the LAP such as to bring it into compliance with the 2000 Act, and where the High Court has granted declaratory relief to that end. It notes that the Council forms part of the local government of the State under Article 28A of the Constitution with responsibility to perform certain functions in the interests of local communities.  The periodic making of an LAP is one such function of the Council that is performed in the interests of the common good for the proper planning and sustainable development of a local area, and is required by law.  

 14.          The appellant submits that the evidence is entirely against the proposition that there is any endemic problem preventing local authorities from preparing LAPs. The issue, according to the appellant, concerns whether the Court should intervene to require the Council to carry out its constitutionally mandated function, when its failure to do so in effect conflicts with the separation of powers between the executive and legislative branches of the State. It submits that the courts are required to intervene via mandamus to maintain the separation of powers. 

 15.          As regards the resource restraints identified by Mr. Russell in his first affidavit on behalf of the Council, the appellant notes how Hogan J. in B. v. Child Family Agency [2025] IESC 2 (" B. "), distinguished Brady on the basis that the road in Brady was just one of hundreds in the same County in a similar state of disrepair, compared with the specific statutory provisions in B. which affected a small cohort of children and were enacted against the backdrop of Article 42A of the Constitution.  The appellant submits that despite the case at hand being distinguishable from Brady , the reasoning does require to be re-assessed.  It argues that the Council's own evidence is that significant resources are clearly being devoted to tasks that are not required by statute, and, in those circumstances, the Council cannot legitimately make a resource argument in relation to statutory non-compliance, where its own evidence is that it has not even attempted to prioritise such statutory work over non-statutory work. 

 16.          The appellant claims that the Council has a duty of candour to explain why LAPs are not being prepared, and why there has been a systematic and subsisting failure to prepare them. It claims to be completely in the dark as to why the Council is relying on resource deficiencies since 2022, in circumstances where it has been in default since 2015 for other plans, and since 2020 for this East Meath LAP. It disputes the reliance by the Council and indeed the trial judge on the failure of the Council to prepare LAPs in these other areas to resist an order for mandamus in respect of the East Meath LAP, on the basis that it would favour one part of the county to the exclusion of the rest. It submits that there is no analogy between a single road in a huge network of roads in various states of disrepair, as in Brady , and statutory plans which are limited in number, and where the timetable for review is foreseeable. If the Council's argument were taken to its logical conclusion, the applicant avers that it would lead to the absurdity that a planning authority which failed to adopt one plan could be subject to an order of mandamus, but where the planning authority failed to adopt multiple plans, it could not. 

 17.          As regards the Council's argument that how to deploy its resources is a matter for wide executive discretion, the appellant asserts that it would turn the concept of the separation of powers on its head to allow a public body itself to breach the separation of powers between it and the Legislature, so that it could choose which statutory obligations to carry out and to assign priorities between various such obligations. 

 18.          The appellant notes that the High Court accepted that the lack of experienced staff and failure of recruitment was "stark" and could be an exceptional circumstance, and Nolan J. accepted the bona fides of the Council that it understands its obligation.  The appellant submits that this is not a question of bona fides or otherwise.  It argues that the High Court let the Council "off the hook" and failed to interrogate how the Council could possibly have achieved this extent and breadth of statutory non-compliance otherwise than by deliberate choice.  

 19.          As regards the trial judge's reliance on Mulhaire and Ward , the appellant submits the Oireachtas had not imposed an obligation on a planning authority to provide a house to a person, but merely provided for the entitlement of a person to have their housing needs assessed. For that reason, in Mulhaire and Ward the Court deemed it inappropriate to intervene to determine how a local authority is to allocate housing. Such a discretion is conferred by the Oireachtas on the local authority, whereas a discretion has not been conferred by the Oireachtas on the Council as to whether and when to prepare LAPs. 

 20.           The appellant argues that the trial judge was in error in misapplying McD , which required detailed evidence that compliance with the statutory duty would be impossible because of restrictions on resources. It argues that the evidence before the High Court in this case showed that the Council opted to prioritise non-statutory work, and that there was no detailed evidence to the effect that it was impossible to comply.  It was clearly possible to prioritise LAPs over non-statutory plans, and there was no evidence prior to 2022 in any case. 

 21.          As regards the issue of prejudice to the appellant, the appellant submits that the trial judge was incorrect in how it addressed same.  Without a LAP, the appellant warns of a highly unregulated planning system with deeply prejudicial effects on affected communities in terms of lack of crucial infrastructure and facilities. This is not a "theoretical" prejudice, as characterised by the trial judge, but a concrete prejudice, and it is submitted that the High Court manifestly erred in determining that in assessing the balance of prejudice, the Council was the "winner".   

 22.          The appellant cites The State (Modern Homes (Ireland) Limited) v Dublin Corporation [1953] I.R. 202 (" Modern Homes "), as particularly instructive.  In that case the planning authority had a statutory obligation to make a planning scheme "with all convenient speed".  The High Court granted an order of mandamus requiring the Council to prepare a planning scheme.  It rejected arguments that "all convenient speed" meant that the Council could proceed at its own pace.  The test for mandamus arising from Modern Homes is helpfully summarised by Barrett J. in O'Donoghue v. The Courts Service [2016] IEHC 262 , and the appellant submits that all of the criteria are satisfied in the present case. 

 23.          The appellant also cites the judgment of Hogan J. in McD , to the effect that the Executive cannot frustrate the exercise of legislative powers by failing to provide requisite resources as would enable the exercise of those powers, or otherwise plead its own failures in this regard as an answer to non-compliance with a statutory obligation. It also relies on the dicta of Hogan J. in B. , to the effect that the Government enjoys no right to suspend or disapply the law, as otherwise it would be tantamount to saying that the Government could in effect secure a repeal of the law without the necessity for legislation. The appellant submits that the intervention sought here is to prevent the Council from arrogating to itself a discretion, where the Oireachtas has definitively decided which statutory obligations should be performed. It is necessary in its submission to uphold the separation of powers by granting an order of mandamus to avoid frustrating the will of the Oireachtas. 

 Submissions of the Respondent 

 24.          The Council states that, although its duties were imposed by the relevant provisions of the 2000 Act, the relief is sought by the appellant pursuant to the High Court's general supervisory jurisdiction. It argues that the Court should exercise its discretion to refuse the application for mandamus on the basis of the exceptional circumstances pleaded in the statement of opposition and verified in the affidavits of Mr. Russell.    

 25.          The Council, having set out the majority judgment of this Court in Brady , argues that an order of mandamus is discretionary in nature, and stresses the effect of such an order in this case, which, it is said, would include the haphazard or arbitrary discharge of its statutory duty to make LAPs within its functional area.  It asserts that it does not seek to make arrangements to relieve itself of the obligations expressly imposed on it by the 2000 Act. Rather, it submits that the granting of an order of mandamus would be ineffectual to secure compliance with the statutory duty, due to exceptional factual and legal circumstances said to pertain. 

 26.          It is submitted that it is necessary to set the context within which the courts may consider discretionary factors in deciding whether to grant or refuse an order of mandamus . The Council submits that the trial judge's approach was consistent with the decision of the UK Supreme Court in R. (Imam) v. London Borough of Croydon [2023] UKSC 45 , which was based on the context, the issues involved and the effect upon the applicant and society as a whole. It contends that the High Court correctly concluded, in exercising its discretion, that it would be unjust to order mandamus , given the exceptional circumstances which pertained.      

 27.          The Council submits that the circumstances which gave rise to the ultimate decision in Modern Homes were correctly distinguished by the trial judge from those in the B case, and are also distinguishable from those in the present case.  It relies on the judgment of Murray J. in McD as indicating that a more nuanced view may be appropriately taken in relation to the separation of powers and the division of institutional competences, which analysis necessarily depends on the facts of the case.   

 28.          While the Council accepts that, pursuant to Article 28A of the Constitution, it is recognised as part of local government, this it is said does not mean that the Court is required to intervene via mandamus to maintain the separation of powers. It states that some steps have been taken to prepare LAPs for other areas ranking in precedence to East Meath, and that it has used its extremely limited staff resources in a rational and fair fashion. It suggests that its commitment to prepare the East Meath LAP has been reiterated in correspondence, and it refutes the appellant's assertions that it has said it is not prepared to take any steps on foot of the conceded declaration. 

 29.          The Council concludes that Brady remains good law and that the High Court judgment does not offend the rule of law or the separation of powers. It asserts that the trial judge did not engage in an exercise of "routinely declining" to grant mandamus on the grounds of absence of sufficient resources; rather, the High Court decided correctly on the basis of the evidence before it that there were exceptional circumstances in this case such as to warrant a refusal of an order of mandamus .   

 Further Evidence 

 30.          In advance of the oral hearing the respondent filed a second affidavit of Alan Russell, the Acting Senior Planner in the Council, sworn on the 8 th October, 2025.  He stated that since the High Court judgment, and indeed in the two week period prior to the swearing of his affidavit, a number of matters had occurred which, he was advised by the Council's solicitor and believed, should be brought to the attention of the Supreme Court.  As regards the issue of staff and recruitment, he stated that in circumstances where the Council had continued to experience staff shortages in its Forward Planning Section, the Council had been unable to advance the preparatory work necessary for aspects of the new Meath CDP or a number of the LAPs identified in the existing CDP.  Accordingly, he went on, in order to progress matters, on the 23 rd September, 2025, the Council published a tender notice in the following terms: 

 "Request for Tenders dated 23/09/2025 for the provision of Consultancy Services for Local Area Plans and Settlement Plans/Written Statements in Development Plans, Urban Area Plans, Priority Area Plans, Urban Development Zones." 

 31.          Mr. Russell exhibited a copy of the said tender notice, which listed the LAP for East Meath as part of the scope of services required under the proposed contract, and which set a tender deadline of the 23 rd October, 2025.  

 Decision 

 32.          It is clear from the above that the net issue arising in this appeal is whether the Court should go further than the declaration granted by the High Court, and should grant an order of mandamus compelling the Council to make an LAP.  

 33.          In any consideration of the question of the extent to which the courts should enforce statutory obligations prescribed by the Oireachtas, the starting point is that in a society governed by democratic values and the rule of law it is the duty of the courts to enforce the law. In the case of local authorities their obligation to obey the law is clearly prescribed by Article 28A.2 of the Constitution: 

 "There shall be such directly elected local authorities as may be determined by law and their powers and functions shall, subject to the provisions of this Constitution, be so determined and shall be exercised and performed in accordance with law ." (emphasis added) 

 34.          It is quite clear, therefore, that there is a constitutional imperative imposed on local authorities to discharge their functions in accordance with law. Here the law has been clearly prescribed by the Oireachtas, and it was not disputed that the Council was under a statutory obligation by virtue of s. 19 of the 2000 Act to prepare a LAP in respect of East Meath. To that extent this case is significantly different from cases involving the exercise of a statutory discretion such as Ward and Mulhaire . In these circumstances one might fairly ask why an order of mandamus should not be made. 

 35.          The first argument advanced by the Council was that the entire LAP structure was scheduled to be dismantled once the relevant provisions of the 2024 Act were commenced. It was said that the preparation of a LAP would be something of a pointless exercise given that these provisions were due to be commenced, perhaps shortly. Like Nolan J. I found myself unimpressed by this argument. This Court must take the law as it finds it, and there is long-standing authority from this Court for the proposition that a public body cannot invoke a justification of this nature as an excuse for its failure to apply the existing law. As Kennedy C.J. remarked in R. (IUDW) v. Rathmines UDC [1928] IR 260 at 297: 

 "...the excuse that there were proposals before the Dáil for an alteration in the law which might, or might not, receive legislative sanction...is not a justification of the appellants' refusal to obey the existing law which a Court can entertain." 

 36.          Similar remarks were made by Maguire C.J. in Modern Homes when he said (at 227): 

 "If the appellants are playing for time in the hope that the difficulties which they have encountered in preparing a planning scheme will be removed by legislation they must understand that such conduct is unwarranted and cannot be accepted by the Court as a valid reason for failure to carry out the plain duty laid upon them by the statute." 

 37.          As of the date of the hearing of this appeal, the repealing provisions of the 2024 Act had not yet been commenced and there was no clear indication that a commencement order was imminent. It might have been different if, for example, a commencement order had been made under the 2024 Act which nominated a particular day for the repeal of the s. 19 LAP obligation, so that the making of an order of mandamus might in such circumstances be regarded as futile. As far as the Court was aware no such commencement order of this kind had been made in respect of these provisions of the 2024 Act and in those circumstances, I would, like Nolan J., have rejected this particular explanation.  I will come on to a more recent post-hearing development later in this judgment. 

 The lack of resources argument 

 38.          The principal argument advanced by the Council in opposing mandamus was that it lacked the appropriate staff and that it found the recruitment of suitable personnel to be difficult.  The first affidavit of Mr. Russell filed on behalf of the Council pointed to the schedule of priorities of the various Meath regions in terms of the preparation of LAPs. The Council considers that it has fairly marshalled its resources so that priority is given to regional growth centres such as South Drogheda and key towns such as Maynooth. Here one must note again that this scheme of priorities is internal to the Council and it enjoys no statutory provenance. 

 39.          The Council pointed to the decision of this Court in Brady in reliance on its argument that a court will not make a coercive order such as mandamus to compel the performance of a statutory duty, where the local authority lacked the funds to do so. In Brady the applicant had sought an order of mandamus requiring the Council to discharge its statutory duty to repair a road which was admittedly in a state of extreme disrepair. The road was, however, just one of hundreds in the same county in a similar state of disrepair and the Council frankly admitted that it did not have the resources to finance the large-scale road repair programme which would have been necessary to enable it to discharge this function. A majority of this Court held that in those circumstances it would be inappropriate to make an order of mandamus. 

 40.          In his judgment for the majority, Keane J. (as he then was) stated as follows (at 103-106): 

 "The order of mandamus , in essence a command issuing from the High Court and directed to a person or body, requiring him or them to do a particular specified act which appertains to his or their office and is in the nature of a public duty, has always been regarded by the law as discretionary in its nature. That was clearly the case with the prerogative writ of mandamus (see Julius v. Lord Bishop of Oxford (1880) 5 App. Cas. 214 at p. 246) and, in my view, remains the law, although the remedy now takes the form of an order of mandamus by way of judicial review.  

 One of the grounds on which the courts decline to exercise their discretion in favour of granting the order was, if established, the futility of so doing.  That, it is claimed on behalf of the respondent, is the position in this case... 

   

 The leading Irish authority on the topic is the decision of the former Supreme Court in... Modern Homes ..., the facts of which are well known and can be shortly summarised.  The defendants, Dublin Corporation, as the planning authority for its area, had resolved to make a planning scheme under the provisions of the Town and Regional Planning Acts, 1934 and 1939.  That entitled them to require buildings erected without its permission in its area to be pulled down or altered.  But also obliged it to make the planning scheme "with all convenient speed" and submit it to the Minister for Local Government for his approval.  Although the defendant had passed the appropriate resolution in 1936, by the year 1950 it had failed to make the development plan and the prosecutor, who had been refused permission for various buildings which it proposed to erect or had been subjected to conditions in respect of their erection, complained that it had been adversely affected in its business operations by the failure of the defendants to make the planning scheme.  Its application for an order of mandamus was resisted on the ground, inter alia , that it would be futile to issue the order.  

   

 Maguire C.J. speaking for the Court...said at p. 229: 

 'It is argued that there can be no certainty that the scheme will be made even if the order of mandamus is issued.  It is, of course, correct that an order will not be made if it is clear that it would be impossible of performance by reason of the circumstances that the doing of the act would involve a contravention of law or if the defendants have not the means of complying with the order...' 

   

 ... 

   

 The learned High Court judge, when she came to consider the practicalities of making the order sought, said: 

 'The Oireachtas having imposed and continued a statutory obligation on a local authority to maintain roads, must, as long as that obligation remains unqualified, make it possible for the local authority to perform its statutory duties. Pre-1978 the local authority would have had to increase its rate to discharge its obligations.  But since the elimination of a broad based rating system it is no longer possible for a County Council to do this.  The central fund therefore must make up the shortfall.  This is not a case of telling the Government how it must spend money.  It is a case of the Oireachtas having imposed a statutory duty on local authorities, being required to provide the means of carrying out that duty.' 

   

 The Oireachtas is not a party to these proceedings and, presumably, having regard to the separation of powers, could not be.  Neither is the Government or the Minister for the Environment.  The Attorney General appeared for the first time in the proceedings in the course of the appeal to this Court and then only in an amicus curiae role.  It may be, for all we know, that these bodies would, in response to the order, provide the respondent with the necessary funds, but neither the judgment in the High Court nor the arguments advanced on behalf of the applicants in this Court offer any guidance as to what is to happen if they do not.  Unless there was coercive authority to the contrary, I would not be disposed to hold that the Court should bring the rigours of mandamus to bear on a public authority where it is acknowledged that it has not the means to comply with the order and that its successful implementation depends on the co-operation of other bodies who are not before the Court." 

 41.          As appears from the above, mandamus , like the other public law remedies, including the declaration and injunction, is a discretionary remedy.  It is clear from Modern Homes , as adopted in Brady , that one of the discretionary bars to relief is that an order will not normally be made if it is clear that it would be impossible of performance by reason of the circumstances that the doing of the act would involve a contravention of law, or if the defendant has not the means of complying with the order.  The grounds on which relief may be denied are, however, not closed, but it is not necessary to set out a complete list of such possible grounds here.  

 Developments since Brady 

 42.          There have, however, been a series of legal developments since this Court gave judgment in Brady in June 1999. In the first place, Article 28A of the Constitution was enacted by the 20th Amendment of the Constitution Act, 1999 about a week after the Supreme Court decision in that case. As I have already observed, it is now clear that local authorities are under a general constitutional obligation to discharge their statutory functions in accordance with law. This is an important - albeit not necessarily decisive - factor which this Court cannot ignore. 

 43.          Secondly, there have been a series of recent decisions of this Court dealing with the care of troubled children which have sought to place Brady in its own particular context: see McD. and B .  Both of these cases involved the question of whether the courts should make coercive orders against the Child and Family Agency to ensure that there were adequate special care places available for the treatment of these troubled children. 

 44.          In McD  Hogan J. contrasted the factual context of that case with that in Brady and stated as follows (at para. 123): 

 "The present case is quite different, in that (unlike Brady ) this case concerns very specific statutory provisions which apply only to a very small cohort of troubled children.  The application of these highly precise statutory provisions cannot realistically be interpreted as being resource dependent and, in any event, they have been enacted against the backdrop of the requirements of Article 42A in order to ensure the best interests of these children.  It may be in any event that aspects of the reasoning in Brady may possibly need to be re-assessed in the light of the contemporary case law dealing with the rule of law and modern separation of powers thinking, but this is something which lies well beyond the parameters of this appeal." 

 45.          Hogan J. made similar observations in a follow-on case, B , where he said (at para. 66) that:  

 "...If it is considered that these statutory provisions impose too great a financial or other burden on the State or its agencies, I repeat that the solution lies in the Oireachtas amending or otherwise diluting the force and reach of these provisions in a manner which is nevertheless consistent with the constitutional rights of the children concerned. Absent such legislative changes it is the clear duty of the Government to comply with the law as enacted by the Oireachtas and as interpreted by the courts." 

 46.          He also stated as follows (at para. 64): 

 "It must be recalled that it is of the essence of the democratic order that the members of the Oireachtas are answerable to the electorate for the legislation which they enact. This means that the Government cannot allow a form of legislative Potemkin village to spring up so that (as here) the impression is created that the Oireachtas has acted decisively in the case of troubled children by providing statutory obligations in respect of special care, while at the same time the effective enforcement of these obligations is prevented or frustrated or is otherwise allowed to lie fallow by Government actions or inactions." 

 47.          If one reviews Brady in the light of the decisions in McD. and B. , it seems to me clear that it must be viewed as an exceptional case where the Council could not realistically have been expected to have discharged its statutory duty, having regard to the funds at its disposal and the sheer scale of the task of repairing hundreds of roads with which it was confronted. To that extent Brady should be seen as the very much the exception and not the norm.  If the position were otherwise, the capacity of the courts to ensure that statutory obligations imposed on public bodies such as local authorities were enforced would otherwise be significantly compromised. This would in turn compromise the rule of the law and the democratic identity of the State as reflected in constitutional provisions such as Article 5, Article 6, Article 15, Article 16 and Article 28A, since it would mean that which the Oireachtas had prescribed as mandatory in the public interest could not be enforced. 

 48.          The present case can, in my opinion, be distinguished from Brady in that the Council does not in terms say that it could not comply with any court order.  Up to recently it simply pointed to the difficulties in the recruitment and retention of experienced staff.  The further evidence put before this Court is highly significant, however, in that the Council has now sought tenders for the provision of consultancy services to make up for staffing deficits and to enable it to discharge certain functions.  One might query why this step was not taken at an earlier stage, in order to enable the Council to comply sooner with its statutory obligations.  In any event there was no suggestion during the oral hearing that the necessary consultancy services would not become available in early course.  

 49.          To this extent, therefore, the present case is much closer to cases such as McD and B , where recruitment and retention of staff issues were also problematic, and indeed arguably more problematic given the further evidence now adduced by the Council. In McD this factor did not, however, deter this Court from making a mandatory order enforcing the public duties which had been imposed on the Child and Family Agency. 

 50.          I do not overlook the fact that an order of this kind may well to some extent disrupt the scheme of priorities which the Council has set for itself, whereby it started with large towns and settlements which were deemed to be the most pressing. Yet these arrangements do not, as such, have any statutory standing: the task of the Council as determined by the Oireachtas is to prepare an LAP for the entirety of its functional area. The Council should not look askance simply because the Court requires it to perform the statutory functions which the Oireachtas, as the democratically elected organ of Government, requires it to discharge. 

 51.          In these circumstances it cannot be said that the present case falls into the exceptional category of cases such as Brady where something close to impossibility was established. The present case falls well short of this.  Furthermore, no other discretionary bar to relief was established by the Council.  

 Post-Hearing Development 

 52.          Subsequent to the hearing of this appeal the Court was notified that, on the 17 th December, 2025, the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage made the Planning and Development Act 2024 (Commencement) (No. 5) Order 2025 (S.I. No. 633 of 2025).  Pursuant to this Order, inter alia , the repeal of the provisions of Chapter II of Part II (including ss. 19 and 20) of the 2000 Act came into operation on the 31 st December, 2025.  The repeal of ss. 19 and 20 of the 2000 Act raises the question as to whether the making of an order of mandamus might in such circumstances now be regarded as inappropriate or futile.  I would invite the parties to make submissions on the orders to be made by the Court in light of this recent development.  

 Conclusion 

 53.          In summary, therefore, I would allow the appeal on the ground that Nolan J. was in error in holding that the Council had excused its failure to comply with its statutory obligations under s. 19(1)(c), s. 20(3)(a)(i) and s. 20(3)(a)(ii) of the 2000 Act. 

 54.          Put simply, the decision in Brady should be regarded as exceptional in that it was all but impossible for the Council in that case to discharge its statutory functions. As befits a democratic State governed by the rule of law, local authorities are required by Article 28A.2 of the Constitution to discharge their statutory functions in accordance with law. Failure to comply with their statutory obligations can be excused only in cases of impossibility or some other wholly exceptional circumstances. For all of the reasons set out above, I am satisfied that the Council cannot point to such circumstances.  

 I would therefore allow this appeal. As stated at para. 52 above, I would invite the parties to make submissions on the orders to be made by the Court in light of the recent change in the legislation.
